stem: You are preparing chat-style training data. How should a single training example be structured?

options.text: One user turn and one assistant turn per example
options.explanation: Splitting a dialogue into pairs would discard the surrounding context the model is meant to learn from.

options.text: A prompt string and a completion string
options.explanation: That shape belongs to the instruction or text dataset types, not to conversational data.

options.text: A nested object keyed by turn index
options.explanation: Ordering comes from the array itself; no index keys are involved.

options.text: One conversation expressed as a single `messages` array
options.explanation: The unit of training is the whole conversation, which is why turns are grouped rather than split into separate examples.

stem: You want a fine-tuned model to be better at calling your tools. What can a training example include to support that?

options.text: A separate tool-schema file referenced by name from the dataset
options.explanation: The definitions travel inside the example itself; there is no external reference mechanism.

options.text: Nothing — tool use cannot be learned through fine-tuning
options.explanation: Tool-augmented conversations are an explicitly supported dataset shape.

options.text: An optional `tools` field declaring the tools available in that conversation
options.explanation: Training on conversations that carry their tool definitions is what teaches the model the calling behaviour you want at inference time.

options.text: A list of example API responses appended after the final turn
options.explanation: Tool results appear as messages within the conversation, not as a trailing appendix.

stem: Your load balancer must decide whether to route traffic to a dedicated endpoint. Which of the two status types should it read?

options.text: Readiness, which reports traffic-serving capability
options.explanation: The two statuses exist precisely so deployment progress and serving capability can be read separately, and routing depends on the latter.

options.text: Lifecycle, which reports deployment state
options.explanation: An endpoint can be mid-deployment and still serving, so lifecycle alone would withhold traffic from a healthy endpoint.

options.text: Either, since they always agree
options.explanation: They routinely differ — that divergence is the reason both are published.

options.text: Both, refusing traffic unless each is in its nominal state
options.explanation: Requiring both would drop traffic during a normal update, when the endpoint is serving perfectly well.

stem: An endpoint reports readiness "Partially ready". What does that tell you?

options.text: It is fully provisioned but has not yet received traffic
options.explanation: Fully provisioned is "Ready". Readiness does not report whether traffic has arrived.

options.text: It is serving traffic, but below expected capacity
options.explanation: Some replicas are still starting, updating or unavailable, so requests succeed while headroom is reduced.

options.text: It is not serving traffic and requests will fail
options.explanation: That is the "Not ready" state. Partially ready still serves.

options.text: Only some model methods are available
options.explanation: Readiness describes capacity across replicas, not a subset of functionality.

stem: Your application defines a `get_weather` tool and the model returns a tool call for it. Which component runs the actual weather lookup?

options.text: Your application, which then passes the result back to the model
options.explanation: The model only emits an invocation instruction. Executing the function and feeding its output back into the next prompt is the application's responsibility.

options.text: The model, which executes the function and returns its output directly
options.explanation: The model never executes anything. It proposes a call; running it is explicitly left to your backend or client.

options.text: The inference endpoint, which proxies the call to the named service
options.explanation: No proxying happens. The endpoint returns tool-call instructions in the response and does not reach out to any external service on your behalf.

options.text: The tool schema registry, once the tool has been registered
options.explanation: Tool schemas describe how a tool should be invoked. They are declarative and there is no registry component that executes anything.

stem: You send a request with several tools defined but do not set `tool_choice`. How does the model decide which tool to use?

options.text: It picks the first tool in the array
options.explanation: Selection is driven by the conversation context, not by the position of a tool in the list.

options.text: It selects the most appropriate tool from the prompt context
options.explanation: Automatic selection based on context is the default, which is why most use cases never need to set the parameter at all.

options.text: It calls every defined tool once and merges the results
options.explanation: Nothing fans a request out across all tools. The model proposes calls it judges relevant, and often none at all.

options.text: It refuses to call any tool until one is named explicitly
options.explanation: Naming a tool explicitly is the override, not the precondition. Without it the model still chooses freely.

stem: How is each available tool described to the model?

options.text: With an OpenAPI document referenced by URL
options.explanation: Tools are declared inline in the request. No external specification is fetched.

options.text: With a Python type signature introspected from the callable
options.explanation: Client libraries may help you generate the schema, but what the API receives is the schema, not a language-specific signature.

options.text: With a JSON Schema giving its name, parameters and data types
options.explanation: The schema is what tells the model how the tool may be invoked, which is why parameter types belong in it rather than in the prompt text.

options.text: With a natural-language description in the system prompt
options.explanation: Prose in the system prompt can add context, but the tool contract itself is structured and machine-readable.

stem: A workflow must always call `read_file` first, regardless of what the user asked. You set `tool_choice` to that function explicitly. What is the effect?

options.text: The model prefers it but may pick another tool if context suggests one
options.explanation: That describes automatic selection. An explicit choice is not a hint.

options.text: The model calls it only if the user request mentions a file
options.explanation: Context ceases to matter once a specific function is named.

options.text: The request fails if another tool would have scored higher
options.explanation: There is no scoring conflict to fail on; the named function is simply the one that gets called.

options.text: The model calls it regardless of context, overriding its own selection
options.explanation: An explicit choice replaces the model's judgement entirely, which is what makes it suitable for a deterministic first step.

stem: A completed fine-tuning job produced several checkpoints. What is a checkpoint?

options.text: The final merged model, one per completed job
options.explanation: If there were only ever one per job, listing them and choosing between them would be pointless.

options.text: The model after a certain number of training steps, often one per epoch
options.explanation: Checkpoints capture the model at intervals during training, which is why more than one exists and why you may prefer an earlier one.

options.text: A snapshot of the training dataset as it was processed
options.explanation: Checkpoints hold model state. The dataset is an input and is not re-snapshotted.

options.text: A log entry marking a stage transition in the job
options.explanation: Stage transitions surface as job events, which are a separate thing to inspect.

stem: A fine-tuning job is running and you want to know whether the dataset was accepted and how training is progressing. What should you inspect?

options.text: The uploaded file's metadata, which records a validation verdict
options.explanation: File metadata describes the upload. The job's view of processing appears in its events.

options.text: The dataset query template, which reports parse errors
options.explanation: Query templates concern reading dataset content, not monitoring a training run.

options.text: Job events, which cover file validation, dataset processing and progress
options.explanation: Events are the running narrative of a job, which is what makes them the right place to look while it is still in flight.

options.text: The checkpoint list, which grows as validation succeeds
options.explanation: Checkpoints tell you what was produced, not whether the input was accepted or where training has got to.

stem: Two teams must not see each other's datasets or endpoints. Which level of the resource model isolates them?

options.text: A project, since resources live inside it and inherit its access settings
options.explanation: Because resources take their access from the enclosing project, giving each team its own project is what produces the isolation.

options.text: The organization, since it is the top of the hierarchy
options.explanation: The organization is the shared container above projects, so placing both teams in one does not separate them.

options.text: The API key, since each key is scoped to a single resource
options.explanation: Keys are issued within a project. They express access, but the project is what bounds it.

options.text: An organization group, since groups own resources directly
options.explanation: Groups configure identity and access for people. Resources belong to projects, not to groups.

stem: What exists immediately after you sign up, before you create anything?

options.text: Nothing until you create an organization yourself
options.explanation: You can create further organizations later, but the first one is not something you have to set up.

options.text: A shared default organization common to all new users
options.explanation: The organization created at signup is yours, not a tenancy shared with strangers.

options.text: A project, with an organization created only when you invite someone
options.explanation: The hierarchy runs organization then project, so the organization cannot appear second.

options.text: A personal organization, created automatically
options.explanation: Signup provisions an organization for you, so there is always a workspace to create projects in.

stem: Latency matters more than token cost for your chat feature. How do you request the Fast flavor of a model?

options.text: Set a `flavor` parameter to `fast` in the request body
options.explanation: There is no flavor parameter. The suffix on the model name is the whole mechanism.

options.text: Deploy a dedicated endpoint configured for low latency
options.explanation: A dedicated endpoint is a different product decision. The Fast flavor is available without one.

options.text: Request a different base URL reserved for latency-sensitive traffic
options.explanation: The base URL is unchanged. Only the model name differs.

options.text: Append `-fast` to the model name in the API request
options.explanation: Flavor selection travels with the model identifier, so no separate parameter or endpoint is involved.

stem: A colleague argues you should not use the Fast flavor because it will change what the model answers. Are they right?

options.text: Yes — speculative decoding trades some accuracy for speed
options.explanation: Speculative decoding is a latency optimization that preserves the output; it does not degrade quality.

options.text: Only for vision models, where the flavors use different weights
options.explanation: Flavors do not swap weights for any modality. The model is the same.

options.text: No — outputs are identical; only pricing, latency and optimizations differ
options.explanation: Flavors are an infrastructure choice. Since outputs match, the decision is purely about cost and responsiveness.

options.text: Yes — smaller batch sizes change the sampling distribution
options.explanation: Batch size affects throughput and latency, not the content of the response.

stem: Your traffic has grown steadily for weeks and you have not asked for a quota increase. What happens to your rate limit?

options.text: It is recalculated monthly from your average consumption
options.explanation: Evaluation happens on a far shorter cycle than a month, which is what lets the limit track a growing workload.

options.text: It rises on its own as you consistently run close to the current cap
options.explanation: Limits are dynamic, so sustained usage near the ceiling is itself the signal that raises it — no ticket required.

options.text: It stays fixed until you request an increase
options.explanation: A static cap is exactly what this system replaces. Requests are only needed beyond the hard ceiling.

options.text: It rises only after you upgrade to the Enterprise tier
options.explanation: Enterprise removes the soft caps, but growth within them happens automatically first.

stem: You want to back off before hitting a limit rather than react to errors. What does the API give you?

options.text: A webhook fired as you approach the cap
options.explanation: No such notification exists. Headroom is reported inline.

options.text: Nothing — you must count requests client-side
options.explanation: Counting locally cannot see a limit that moves, which is precisely why the values are returned to you.

options.text: Remaining-request and remaining-token response headers
options.explanation: Because the headers ride on every response, you can steer on live headroom instead of waiting for a rejection.

options.text: A quota endpoint you poll on a schedule
options.explanation: Polling a separate endpoint would lag your actual consumption; the data arrives with the responses themselves.

stem: A request that exceeded your rate limit succeeded anyway, carrying an over-limit response header. Why?

options.text: The limit had already scaled up in the current window
options.explanation: Had the limit risen, the request would not have been over it, and no over-limit header would appear.

options.text: Header-only mode was enabled, so limits are advisory
options.explanation: There is no advisory mode. Limits are enforced; this is an exception made when capacity allows.

options.text: The request was queued and retried automatically after the window reset
options.explanation: Nothing is held and replayed. It was processed at the time, just with lower priority.

options.text: Spare capacity let it run at lower priority without affecting others
options.explanation: Over-limit processing is opportunistic, so it depends on capacity that happens to be free rather than on anything about your request.

stem: You need a model to return data your code can parse without a post-processing step. Which request parameter controls this?

options.text: `output_schema`
options.explanation: No such parameter exists. A schema is supplied inside `response_format`, not as a sibling of it.

options.text: `content_type`
options.explanation: Content type belongs to HTTP headers and describes the transport, not the shape of the generated content.

options.text: `strict_mode`
options.explanation: Strictness is expressed by choosing the schema-following type, not by a separate boolean parameter.

options.text: `response_format`
options.explanation: This is the parameter that switches a model from prose to JSON, and its type field selects which of the two JSON modes applies.

stem: You want valid JSON but do not care about the exact field names. Which `response_format` type fits, and what are you giving up?

options.text: `json_object` — but the output may still be prose
options.explanation: The mode forces JSON output. What it does not constrain is which fields appear.

options.text: `text` with a JSON instruction in the prompt
options.explanation: Prompting alone provides no guarantee of parseable output, which is the reason the dedicated modes exist.

options.text: `json_object` — the model chooses the schema itself
options.explanation: This mode guarantees the output parses as JSON while leaving its shape to the model, so downstream code cannot rely on specific keys.

options.text: `json_schema` — the model chooses the schema itself
options.explanation: Schema-following mode is the opposite case: you supply the schema and the output conforms to it.

stem: You already pass a JSON schema in `response_format` but output quality is inconsistent. What does the documentation recommend?

options.text: Lower the temperature until output stabilises
options.explanation: Sampling parameters are not the documented remedy here, and they do not address whether the model understood the target shape.

options.text: Split the schema into several smaller requests
options.explanation: Decomposition is a general engineering tactic, not the guidance given for structured output quality.

options.text: Switch to arbitrary JSON mode and validate afterwards
options.explanation: That discards the constraint you wanted. The advice is to reinforce the schema, not abandon it.

options.text: Also state the schema and the JSON instruction in the prompt
options.explanation: Repeating the instruction and schema in the system or user prompt is the documented way to improve quality and consistency.
